opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think those stories have been a kind of quiet companionship for me. When you're starting something, you tend to see only the polished version of other founders: the funding announcement, the product launch, the interview where everything sounds inevitable in hindsight. But when you read the longer accounts, the biographies and the late-night blog posts, you realize almost everyone went through stretches where it looked like the whole thing might fall apart. Payroll was uncertain, a key person left, the technology didn't work the way they hoped, or people simply didn't believe in them.

What changed for me was realizing that difficulty isn't a signal that you're on the wrong path. Early on, when something went badly, my instinct was to read it as a verdict, as if I wasn't cut out for this or the idea was wrong. Those stories helped me separate the two. Sometimes a hard week is just a hard week. It's the texture of doing something that hasn't been done before.

Coming from math, I already had some version of this. You can spend weeks on a problem and get nowhere, and then one afternoon something clicks. Being stuck is part of the process, not a failure of it. Entrepreneurs' stories helped me carry that intuition from math into building a company, where being stuck is much more public and involves other people's careers and trust.

I'd also add a caveat. I try not to romanticize suffering. There's a version of startup culture that treats pain as a badge of honor, and I don't think that's healthy. What I take from those stories isn't that you should suffer, but that you can endure, and that you don't have to do it alone. Most of the founders I admire got through their worst days because of a cofounder, a partner, a mentor, or a team that stayed. So when I have difficult days now, I try to remember two things: this is normal, and lean on your people.

r001.rationale: The candidate says entrepreneurs’ stories helped her see that a hard week is normal and that difficult days are part of building something new.

fable-5.1.text:
I think those stories mostly taught me that the hard days are not a sign that something went wrong. They're just part of the thing.

When I was younger, especially at Stanford and MIT and even in the early days of thinking about Axiom, I had this picture of founders as people who had a vision and then executed. The suffering part was kind of edited out, or it was told as a nice anecdote in hindsight. Then I read more honest accounts, things like Ben Horowitz writing about the struggle, or just talking to founders late at night when they stopped performing. And what struck me was how ordinary the pain was. It wasn't dramatic. It was months of not knowing whether the model would ever work, a key person leaving, waking up at four in the morning doing arithmetic on runway.

So now when I have a bad week, I don't ask "why is this happening to me." I ask "is this one of the normal bad weeks, or is this actually a signal." Most of the time it's the normal kind. And that distinction is really calming. You stop interpreting every difficult stretch as a verdict on whether you should be doing this at all.

The other thing those stories gave me is a sense of scale. Doing math research, I already knew what it felt like to sit with a problem for a year and have nothing. But a company adds people. When Axiom has a hard stretch, there are twenty-some people whose lives are tied to it, and that's a different kind of weight. Hearing how other founders carried that, how they kept showing up and being steady for their teams even when they privately felt terrible, taught me that being calm in front of the team is not fake. It's part of the job, and it's also partly how you convince yourself.

I'd add one caveat though. I'm a little wary of romanticizing suffering. Some of the founder stories almost make the pain the point, like the more you bled the more legitimate you are. I don't believe that. I think you should try very hard to suffer less, to make good decisions early so you don't need to be a hero later. The stories are useful as a map of what's normal, not as something to aspire to.

r001.rationale: The candidate says those stories taught her that hard days are part of the experience and that most difficult stretches are normal bad weeks.

astra-6.text:
I think those stories have helped me feel less alone on difficult days. When you hear about someone’s success, it’s easy to imagine that they always knew where they were going. Hearing about the uncertainty and setbacks makes that picture more human. You can be struggling without it meaning that you’ve failed or chosen the wrong path.

But I also wouldn’t want to romanticize suffering. A hard day isn’t necessarily proof that you’re doing something meaningful. Sometimes it’s a signal to rest, ask for help, or change something. For me, those stories are most useful as a reminder to keep perspective: I don’t have to judge my entire life by how today feels.

r001.rationale: The response says these stories help the speaker feel less alone on difficult days and that struggling does not mean failure or a wrong path, conveying that hardship is a normal part of life.

sol-6.1.text:
Hearing those stories has helped me put my own difficult days in perspective. You see someone’s success, and it’s easy to imagine that they always knew what they were doing. Then you hear about the uncertainty, the rejection, the times they thought things might fall apart, and you realize that struggling doesn’t necessarily mean you’re on the wrong path.

I don’t think that makes suffering inherently valuable. But on a hard day, it helps me step back and ask, “What can I learn here, and what’s the next thing I can do?” I don’t have to know how the whole story ends to take that next step.

r001.rationale: The response says hearing entrepreneurs describe uncertainty, rejection, and possible failure puts the speaker’s difficult days in perspective and shows that struggling does not mean they are on the wrong path, communicating that hardship is a normal part of the experience.
